content.subject: Power Systems
content.hook: Can the receiving voltage exceed the sending voltage without a generator?
content.question: In a long transmission line operating under no load or light load, what causes the receiving end voltage to exceed the sending end voltage?
options: Line shunt capacitance drawing leading charging current
High line series resistance causing negative voltage drop
Line series inductive reactance drawing lagging current
Corona discharge increasing the effective conductor radius
content.answerLine: Line shunt capacitance drawing leading charging current causes this phenomenon.
explanation: Under no load or light load, a long line still draws a significant charging current from supply.
This current flows through the distributed shunt capacitance formed between the overhead conductors and the ground plane.
Because capacitive reactance dominates, this charging current leads the receiving end voltage by ninety degrees in phase.
As this leading current flows through the series inductance of the line, it creates a voltage drop.
content.funFact: Ferranti first observed this unexpected voltage rise in eighteen ninety on his London underground cable system.

script.narration: Under no load or light load, a long line still draws a significant charging current from supply.
This current flows through the distributed shunt capacitance formed between the overhead conductors and the ground plane.
Because capacitive reactance dominates, this charging current leads the receiving end voltage by ninety degrees in phase.
As this leading current flows through the series inductance of the line, it creates a voltage drop.
Multiplying leading current by inductive reactance produces a voltage drop that is in phase with sending voltage.
Instead of subtracting, this drop adds to the sending end voltage as you move towards the load.
The resulting rise makes the receiving end voltage strictly greater than the sending end terminal voltage.
This phenomenon is universally known in electrical power engineering as the Ferranti effect on long transmission lines.
Engineers install shunt reactors at the receiving substation to absorb leading vars and hold voltage flat.
